title: Starbloom and the Lost Wishes
markdown:
A meadow lay under the softest moonlight, and Starbloom the unicorn often wandered there. Her mane fell like a silvery waterfall. Her feet made no sound on the dew. Her coat held the quiet of new snow. Willow the robin, a small flutter with a breast as red as a ripe berry, liked to perch on Starbloom’s horn, tiny claws tickling moonlight-white fur.

One evening the last blush of sunset left, and shy stars began to wink. Among the clover, where beetles kept a low hum, and under sleepy daisy heads, Starbloom saw tiny shimmering things. They looked like lost petals, yet they pulsed with a gentle light and a quieter tune.

Willow tilted her head. “What are these little glimmers, like fallen stars?”

Starbloom lowered her nose. Her eyes were calm as a midnight lake. “I believe they are lost wishes. Wishes that drifted from dreamers who were sad or weary.” She nudged one. It brightened, as if it remembered a happy thought. “We must gather them. Every wish deserves a chance to be remembered.”

Their quiet work began. Willow’s sharp eyes missed little. She darted under a dock leaf, then along a beetle-path, and nudged glimmers toward Starbloom as if they were shy guests. Starbloom had brought a small woven pouch lined with moss from the shady side of the oldest oak, and dewdrops that sparkled like captured stars. The pouch smelled of rain and patience. Each time Willow chirped a find, Starbloom scooped with care, never pinching, never hurrying a light that had already been hurried once.

“This one feels like a wish for a warm hug,” she murmured, a rosy light into the pouch.

“And this, by the dandelion, feels like a wish for a sunny day,” Willow said, pointing with her beak.

They found a pale one caught in a spider’s unused corner, and a blue-white one that had hidden under a pebble as if ashamed. Starbloom waited until the pebble agreed to roll. Willow sang a two-note encouragement that was not quite a song and not quite a question.

They moved like a slow dance, grace and bustle sharing the same grass. A fox paused at the hedge, saw they were not hunting, and went on. The meadow seemed to watch. Moonlight grew milky. The dewdrops in the pouch gleamed in a little string. When the pouch grew gently heavy, Starbloom did not boast. She only breathed, and Willow settled on the horn for three steps of rest.

“Now what shall we do with them?” Willow asked, her small heart full.

Starbloom looked at the star-dusted sky, where the constellations had begun their slow waltz. “We will send them home.” She lifted her head. For a moment the beam did not come, and Willow held very still, as if stillness could help. Then a wise old star remembered its job, and a steady path ran from the pouch in Starbloom’s mouth up into the dark. She tipped the pouch a little, then a little more. The wishes floated, twinkling, joining their fellow lights, each a tiny beacon on a moonbeam road. One lingered, shy, until Willow chirped it courage.

When the last one rose, a warm glow lingered, then thinned, then became only ordinary moonlight, which was still a great deal. Crickets began a lullaby they had been saving. Night-blooming jasmine opened and gave the air its sweetest work. A moth wrote a slow letter above the clover and did not wait for a reply. Dew had begun again, as if the meadow were practising morning early. Starbloom nuzzled Willow. They did not make a speech about hope. They lay down in the cool grass, silver coat and small warm bird, and let the meadow keep them, pouch empty, horn tickled, sky a little more complete.

And so wishes that wander still find the sky, if friends gather them gently and tip them toward the star that remembers the way.
